To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Facebook use is associated with improvements in subjective well-being, 2) this association depends on communication type and tie strength, 3) receiving one-click feedback from weak ties is associated with decreases in subjective well-being.

(a) receiving composed communication from strong-ties was associated with improved well-being; (b) sending composed messages was not associated with well-being; (c) receiving broadcast messages and receiving one-click messages were not associated with well being; (d) sending one-click messages was associated with improved wellbeing.

the association between Facebook use and well-being is moderated by the type and strength of communication, with positive associations for receiving composed, targeted communication from strong ties and negative associations for viewing friends’ wide-broadcasts and receiving one-click communication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the use of online communication technologies affects the well-being of their users.
how social media use affects psychological well-being, and how the effects depend on communication type and tie strength.
the role of online interactions in people’s social lives.
